# Density plots {#sec-density-plots}


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_wired(
    base_size = 15))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_wired()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_wired()`, built from the WIRED (US) November/December 2024 cover: a black background, a white frame and bold Helvetica Neue title, and red, blue, pink, gray, and steel blue marks.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
wired_stories <- tibble(
  story_id = 1:400,
  format = sample(c("news", "feature"), size = 400, replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.65, 0.35)),
  minutes = round(if_else(format == "news", 
    rnorm(400, mean = 6, sd = 1.5), 
    rnorm(400, mean = 30, sd = 7)))
)
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```

::::

## Description

A density plot shows where numbers fall, using a line instead of bars. A bar graph of the same numbers splits the `x` axis into boxes and shows how many numbers fall in each box.

```{r}
#| label: describe_bars_density
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
ggplot(data = wired_stories, aes(x = minutes)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0, fill = NA, 
    color = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) + 
  labs(x = NULL)
```

A hill[^hill] is a line that is high in the middle and low on both sides. Instead of boxes, a density plot [puts a small hill over each number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_density_estimation) and adds the hills together into one line. 

```{r}
#| label: describe_curve_density
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
ggplot(data = wired_stories, aes(x = minutes)) + 
  geom_density() + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) + 
  labs(x = NULL)
```

The area under the full line adds up to one,[^area-one] so the line is high where numbers are likely and low where they are not. We can show more than one line in the same graph to compare groups; each group gets its own color, and a key tells us which color goes with which group.



## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
WIRED is a set of stories about computers and the people who use them, put out each month since 1993. Picture one month of WIRED stories: lots of short news stories, plus a smaller number of long stories. We'll make up[^simulate] the reading times of 400 stories in two steps. First, `sample()` picks whether each story is a news story or a long story. Then `rnorm()` picks a reading time from the hill that goes with that kind of story.[^normal] Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 400 stories every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1993) # same 400 stories every time the code runs
wired_stories <- tibble(
  story_id = 1:400, # 400 different stories, one row each
  format = sample(
    c("news", "feature"), # each story is a news post or a feature
    size = 400, # one format for each story
    replace = TRUE, # formats repeat across stories
    prob = c(0.65, 0.35) # about two thirds are news posts
    ),
  minutes = round(
    if_else(format == "news",
      rnorm(400, mean = 6, sd = 1.5), # news posts center on 6 minutes
      rnorm(400, mean = 30, sd = 7) # features center on 30 minutes
      )
    )
)
glimpse(wired_stories)
```
:::

## Distribution

Every graph we've seen so far has one high point.[^peak] Real numbers don't always work that way, and the WIRED stories show why: they have two high points, one for news stories and one for long stories. A density plot is good at showing two high points, but a single number that stands for all the stories[^summary] can miss them completely. Below we'll move from the reading times, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten stories.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(wired_stories, 10)
```
:::

The reading times fall into two groups: news stories between 3 and 8 minutes, and long stories at 17 and 43 minutes. Nothing in this first ten takes between 9 and 16 minutes. The median is the middle number when you put all the numbers in order. Now look at what the mean and median say about all 400 stories.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
wired_stories |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(minutes), 
    median = median(minutes), 
    stories_12_to_18_min = sum(minutes >= 12 & minutes <= 18))
```
:::

The mean reading time is about 15 minutes, but only `r sum(wired_stories$minutes >= 12 & wired_stories$minutes <= 18)` of the 400 stories take between 12 and 18 minutes to read. The mean describes almost none of the stories.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model shows the stories as two parts of one whole. News stories make up about two thirds of the bar.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bar_model_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
wired_stories |> 
  count(format) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = "400 stories", fill = format)) + 
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", 
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) + 
  labs(x = "Number of stories", y = NULL, fill = "Format")
```
:::

The density plot below shows the reading times for each kind of story as its own line. The news line is high and not very wide (most news stories take close to 6 minutes), and the long story line is low and wide (the time to read a long story changes more). The broken line marks the mean reading time, which falls in the low place[^valley] between the two high points.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggplot(data = wired_stories, 
    aes(x = minutes)) + 
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count), fill = format), 
    alpha = 0.6, color = NA) + 
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count)), fill = NA) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(wired_stories$minutes), linetype = "dashed") + 
  labs(x = "Reading time (minutes)", y = "Stories per minute", fill = "Format")
```
:::

The line that runs over the top of both colored areas is what `geom_density()` shows for all 400 stories together. It finds the same two high points, but it uses a hill of the same size for every story,[^bandwidth] so the news hill comes out lower and wider than the news line. You can change how wide the hills are with `adjust`[^adjust] (for example, `geom_density(adjust = 0.5)`).

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Our two steps [put two hills together into one line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixture_distribution).[^mixture] Each story's reading time comes from one of the two hills, picked 65 times out of 100 for news and 35 times out of 100 for long stories:[^prob]

$$
f(x) = 0.65 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 6, 1.5) + 0.35 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 30, 7)
$$

The first numbers (0.65 and 0.35) set how much area each hill gets, the middle numbers (6 and 30) set where each hill stands, and the last numbers (1.5 and 7) set how wide each hill is.[^params] The mean of the full line is the mean of the two middle numbers, with each one given its share:[^weighted] $0.65 \times 6 + 0.35 \times 30 = 14.4$ minutes. That's why the mean lands in the low place between the hills.

Try moving the two middle numbers closer together in `rnorm()`. Once the hills cover enough of each other, the low place goes away and the line looks like it has one high point, even though the numbers still come from two groups.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}

Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data`

Put `minutes` on the `x` axis

Add `geom_density()` on top[^layer]

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
One problem with a density plot is that the numbers on the `y` axis are hard to read.

The numbers on the `y` axis are not a number of stories. They show how much of the area under the line stands over each minute,[^density-y] and all of that area adds up to one. That is why the numbers are so small, and why they would change if we gave the reading times in hours instead of minutes. Most people read a density plot by where the line is high and where it is low, not by these numbers. Taking the numbers away keeps people looking at the line, so it's common to take the `y` axis off with `scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)`.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: create_graph_density_no_y
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density() +
      scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```
:::

[^hill]: A hill stands in for the kernel, the small curve `geom_density()` places over each value. The default is a Gaussian (normal) kernel, which is bell shaped.

[^area-one]: The total probability under a density curve is 1.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^simulate]: Simulate.

[^normal]: A normal distribution with its own mean and standard deviation (the `mean` and `sd` arguments in `rnorm()`).

[^seed]: Setting the random seed.

[^peak]: A peak, or mode. A distribution with two peaks is bimodal.

[^summary]: Summary statistics, like the mean and median.

[^formula]: The formula.

[^valley]: The valley between the two peaks.

[^bandwidth]: The bandwidth. `geom_density()` uses one bandwidth for all values, chosen with `bw = "nrd0"` by default.

[^adjust]: The `adjust` argument multiplies the bandwidth; values below 1 make each hill narrower.

[^mixture]: A mixture distribution.

[^prob]: Probabilities of 0.65 and 0.35.

[^params]: The weights, means, and standard deviations of the two normal distributions.

[^weighted]: A weighted average.

[^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, and axis titles).

[^layer]: Add the `geom_density()` layer.

[^density-y]: The probability density. Its units are 1 per minute, so the values change when the units on the `x` axis change.
